cells: FIRST EXPLORATION  |  Make the diagram or calculation earn its place
Core rule: BEFORE—why show it and define terms; DURING—present clearly; AFTER—interpret evidence and say WHAT MATHEMATICS COMES NEXT.
Personalise 1–3 optional suggestions from aim, IA route, beneficiary, prediction, data readiness, variable types, course maths and the student's first-action plan.
Don't teach below-course procedures in the IA (how to draw a bar chart, how to plot a scatter diagram). Explain WHY this choice is useful and what it reveals.

Every figure should fit on ONE printed page. Pathfinder editorial preference: avoid lengthy raw-data tables even in appendices; necessary supporting data can be placed in a well-referenced appendix; this is not an IB prohibition. Don't repeat redundant figures.
If no figure advances the story, select a short first calculation or case, or skip. Suggestions are not evidence, automatic calculations or teacher approval.
First diagram, short calculation or case
Why it helps the IA story
Two numerical variables; linear/positive/negative/unknown relationship predicted
A clear labelled scatter diagram of ACTUAL paired observations
See whether a relationship looks broadly linear, curved, clustered or absent, so the next analysis follows the evidence.
Introduce the two defined quantities and units first; state why seeing association matters to the aim.
Observed direction/shape, unusual points or lack of a clear trend—not a result promised in advance.

If ACTUALLY roughly linear, consider if PMCC would add useful quantification; if unmistakably straight, PMCC may add little. If curved or no pattern, select a more suitable evidence-led next question. Student decides.
Do not explain HOW to plot points at length; PMCC-specific weaknesses only if PMCC is later used.
One scatter diagram showing the whole relevant range
Distinguish possible curve, monotonic trend or distinct groups from a straight-line assumption.
Define and label each numerical variable before plotting; cite source if secondary.
Genuine curvature or change in slope if supported by the data.

Choose a mathematically suitable nonlinear relationship, or for genuinely monotonic data a course-appropriate rank measure if needed; don't assume every curved pattern needs Spearman or a specific model.
Do not present multiple near-identical scatter diagrams just to illustrate different tentative explanations.
Distribution, normal, skew or cluster prediction
A readable histogram OR compact distribution summary if a graph adds value
See overall shape, skewness, possible peaks and spread before choosing a model or summary statistic.
Define measured quantity/unit and explain why its distribution informs the aim.
Actual skew, spread or unusual clusters if present.
Choose appropriate descriptive measures or investigate whether a particular distribution model is reasonable later.
Don't assume normality; avoid overly fine bins implying false measurement accuracy.
Two+ groups with the same quantitative variable; predicted difference in average/spread
Side-by-side box plots, dot plots or other suitable common-scale comparison
Make a single fair comparison of location, spread and unusual values.
Define variable/unit and group labels before figure; describe how groups were formed.
Whether any group difference or variability is actually visible.
Consider numerical comparison of means/medians/spread; a statistical test only if taught, appropriate and now needed.
Do NOT use separated repeated figures with mismatched scales; keep comparison side by side.
Two categorical variables or group proportions
Small two-way frequency/relative-frequency summary OR a useful proportion bar comparison
See whether category proportions differ before choosing any inferential method.
Define categories and denominators; identify population/subgroups.
Differences in relative proportions, if supported by adequate counts.
Compute meaningful conditional proportions; later consider an appropriate chi-squared test ONLY if relevant/available.
No long raw response table; short contingency tables allowed when essential. Don't disguise small category counts.
Counts of success across fixed trials; binomial considered
Short observed success-count frequency summary or one small chart
Visualise observed outcome distribution before testing whether a model might suit.
Define success, number of trials and units for counted outcomes.
Actual frequency shape and range across trials.
Consider whether a binomial model is sensible when calculating probabilities later.
Don't invent trial frequencies or force a plot if a simple calculation is clearer.
Time-ordered data, seasonal pattern or trend suspected
Single labelled line/scatter time plot, using observed times
Distinguish change over time from variation or apparent cycles.
Define t or other meaningful symbol, time units and what one reading represents.
Rate changes, outliers or repeating behaviour if actually seen.
Compare candidate trend/seasonal descriptions, then choose relevant maths.
Only join points if time sequence and interpolation justify it; no repetitive versions.
Large published dataset or subset chosen
A carefully selected short summary and ONE meaningful chart
Show the most relevant structure from the source without burying the IA in raw data.
State source/citation, variables, units, scope and selection criteria BEFORE chart.
Observed distribution, relationship or group contrast within selected subset.
Select the first mathematical question supported by the source.

Prefer a traceable lawful source instead of a huge reproduced table. Pathfinder discourages long appendices; if evidence/reproducibility genuinely requires one, refer to school/teacher guidance rather than claiming IB forbids it.
Constant rate or linear relationship expected; paired observations or parameters available
Short representative rate/difference calculation OR scatter diagram
See whether roughly equal changes over equal intervals support a linear model.
Define variables such as t=time and d=distance with units and meaningful physical domain.
Differences or trend in real readings, not guaranteed constant rate.
Construct or assess a linear function only if meaningful given evidence.
No derivation of how to draw a scatter plot; no unwarranted decimal precision.
Fixed percentage change or exponential growth suspected
Time plot OR calculation comparing percentage changes over a few relevant intervals
Test whether absolute vs relative change seems more stable, so the model form is motivated.
Explain meaning and units of measured quantity and time intervals.
Decide whether exponential vs linear behaviour warrants exploration.
Don't assert exponential growth solely from prediction; avoid long arithmetic demonstrations.
One neat labelled sketch and first relationship between dimensions/constraints
Make clear what is fixed, what can vary, and which quantity may be optimised.
Define L,w,h or equally meaningful symbols and their units BEFORE the drawing.
Geometry and constraints rather than a fabricated optimum.
Form a suitable area/volume/cost expression, then investigate maxima/minima in substantive mathematics.
A decorative repeated drawing adds nothing; don't explain how to sketch a rectangle.
One measured time-series plot covering as much meaningful cycle evidence as available
See whether periodicity is plausible and what period/amplitude might require investigation.
Define time and dependent quantity with units and source.
Observed cycles or too little evidence; either is informative.
If appropriate, test a periodic model and estimate relevant parameters.
Don't label a partial wave as definitely sinusoidal; no unneeded repeated plots.
Positions/times or distances measured in an experiment
One labelled time-position diagram OR short representative differences calculation
Reveal trend and choose between a model for position, speed or change.
Define t and d/s consistently; measurement resolution must inform scale and digits.
Whether changes per interval appear stable or variable.
Select rate-of-change analysis when there is actually enough evidence.
No calculation of acceleration from fabricated or improperly precise readings.
Geometry and measurements needed for area, volume or material models
Single labelled object/scale sketch showing only important dimensions
Explain geometry, dimensional assumptions and which values calculations will use.
Define h=height, r=radius etc. with correct units before use.
Clear constraints or what must be calculated.
Build appropriate dimensional/volume relationship, then check accuracy and assumptions later.
Don't clutter sketch with every unnecessary detail, or show duplicate perspectives without benefit.
Simple accurately labelled map/point plot of actual locations
Help reader see why distance regions might help answer the decision problem.
Define place locations, coordinate units and what 'nearest' is supposed to mean.
Spatial arrangement and plausible boundary questions.
Investigate partitions/distances in substantive mathematics, checking relevance of metric.
No decorative map or one that obscures scale; a full Voronoi analysis needn't be done in the introduction.
No-data mathematical pattern, examples or proof route
One small labelled example, counterexample or short exact calculation
Make the conjecture concrete before attempting general mathematics.
Define mathematical objects, conditions and symbols BEFORE the example.
What the example illustrates—and crucially what it does NOT prove.
Formulate a precise claim and pursue proof/counterexample or extend valid cases.
No invented dataset, no requirement for a statistical plot. Examples alone aren't a general proof.
Pure geometry or algebra uses a meaningful configuration
One clean labelled diagram OR a minimal worked special case
Make the relationships or constraints clear so the next deduction is motivated.
Define meaningful variables and relevant theorems only when first needed.
Relationships or cases that suggest a next mathematical question.
Derive a useful formula/relation or check scope of a conjecture.
Don't require a figure when a concise symbolic example is clearer.
Data not yet obtained, permission pending, or only a plan exists
Choose a permitted simple prototype/illustrative case, OR choose 'Not ready'
Find a safe first mathematical move without pretending actual data already exist.
Clearly label any illustrative values as hypothetical; note pending permissions.
What a method might reveal, not a claim about actual results.
Return to data collection when appropriate or work on a justified abstract case.
Never invent collected data or label the stage complete solely from Planning.
Existing data or mathematical context where a picture adds little
One short meaningful calculation or precise statement, with no figure
Move the mathematics forward with less clutter than a decorative chart.
Define symbols, state aim-linked purpose and write the essential calculation concisely.
Result and its limitations if calculable.
Explain the next question this result raises.
Skip diagram-specific checks; no penalty for choosing none.
DIAGRAM CHECKLIST  |  Show diagram-only checks only when a diagram exists
Have I told the reader WHY this figure is being included before they see it?
One sentence linking figure to aim or decision
Are all variables and specialist words defined before their FIRST appearance in this diagram?
Symbols such as h=height (m), t=time (s) introduced in text
Define symbols/terms before figure, not only in a glossary after it
Don't automatically use x and y
Is there a specific, descriptive title or numbered caption saying WHAT the figure is?
Provide figure label and explanatory caption
Can reference a figure later without repeating it
Does every axis have a meaningful quantity name (not just x or y)?
Height, Time, Distance etc. where appropriate
No axis check for unscaled schematic diagram
Are axes' units included and consistent with the data and calculations?
Put units on labels and check conversions
Do not assume all quantities have units
Is the scale sensible, easy to read and not misleading?
Useful intervals, equal increments as appropriate, no odd gaps
Zero baseline matters for bar lengths; scatter scales need context, not always zero
Are like-for-like quantities compared on SAME scales and units?
Side-by-side plots or one carefully keyed combined graph
Align axes or explicitly explain why different scales cannot match
Prefer direct juxtaposition to duplicate figures scattered through IA
Will the ENTIRE figure fit on a SINGLE printed sheet/page?
Print/PDF preview shows figure + essential caption together, no split
Resize/reposition sensibly; never split a diagram across pages
Do not shrink labels to unreadable size just to fit
Is the figure large enough to read comfortably when printed?
Text, ticks, points/lines/legend legible at page scale
A massive almost-empty chart isn't better than a well-sized one
Does it look good: clean, aligned and visually balanced?
No clipped text, messy annotations, awkward whitespace or crowding
Remove clutter, harmonise sizes and placement
'Looks good' is backed by concrete readability checks, not decoration
Are colours/markers clear and necessary, including in greyscale if printed?
Contrast sufficient; not colour alone for distinction
Avoid gratuitous 3D effects and rainbow palettes
Is there a clear, non-redundant key/legend where needed?
Label on plot or add compact legend
Don't add a redundant legend for a single unambiguous series
Does plotted precision match actual data resolution/uncertainty?
Tick labels and annotations don't claim impossible decimals; plotted positions meaningful
Adjust labels/annotation precision; keep internal calculation guard digits
C24 reported precision and source accuracy
Graph cannot magically improve weak measurement data
Are points, lines or interpolation shown in a way the data justify?
Line connections represent meaningful sequence/assumed continuity
Separate observations or clarify fitted trend
Do not connect unrelated categories with a smooth curve
Are the representation conventions appropriate to the data?
Categorical bar lengths from zero; sensible intervals for numerical histograms
Correct bar baseline or bins; if unequal histogram widths, use suitable frequency-density approach
Categorical vs numerical data and course techniques
Don't confuse bar charts with histograms
Is the source/provenance shown if it isn't the student's own data?
A concise data-source citation and relevant date/selection info
Add short citation close to display
Does it answer a question or motivate a NEW one?
Student can point to one meaningful thing figure adds
Remove it or change approach if it contributes nothing
Am I showing nearly the same diagram more than once?
One figure already presents same data and point
Exception: meaningful direct side-by-side comparison with compatible scales
If repeated/alternative versions are necessary, are they shown together for a specific comparison?
Same page, aligned/same units and scales where appropriate
Put matched versions next to each other and state what differs
Do not reinsert duplicate separated charts
Have I avoided lengthy raw-data tables in the main body and (as a Pathfinder presentation preference) the appendix?
Use a concise selection/summary plus a traceable source where possible; if additional data genuinely aid reproducibility, consult current teacher guidance.
Replace rows of raw data with concise summary; cite appropriate accessible source/dataset separately
Not an IB rule: necessary supporting data can appear in a referenced appendix. Pathfinder discourages clutter, not necessary evidence.
Have I written WHAT I actually observe and explained how this relates to my aim and original prediction?
One or two evidence-linked observations, with honest Supports/Challenges/Unclear where applicable
If surprising, say exactly what differs and what could be checked; do not quietly move on
Actual result, original aim/prediction, intended beneficiary
Don't spend paragraphs teaching bar-chart/scatter construction
Is the conclusion as accurate/reliable as I suggest, or has this already been justified earlier?
Refer to previous source/resolution note when adequate; explain only a NEW issue
Avoid repeated limitations and invented uncertainties; qualify the inference when needed
PMCC/test weaknesses wait until that method is actually used
Does the actual observation lead to a clear NEXT mathematical question, and have I explained WHY?
A justified next action, ideally from the observed feature rather than merely planned maths
A surprising result deserves an alternative/check before blindly proceeding
No unexplained leap into disconnected mathematics
Would the reader lose anything important if I removed this figure?
If no, the diagram may be superfluous
Remove or replace it with a sentence/short calculation
Do not treat diagram count as marks
SHORT INITIAL CALCULATIONS  |  Use instead of a diagram when more useful
Is a brief calculation actually more useful than a diagram here?
Choose short calculation or simple case instead of forcing a chart.
Have I stated what question this calculation helps answer?
One sentence linking to the investigation aim/prediction and next step.
Are symbols and units defined before use?
Use h for height etc., with meaning and units.
Do not default to unnamed x/y
Is the calculation presented clearly and accurately without unnecessary elementary steps?
Show key setup/substitution/result; routine arithmetic does not need several paragraphs.
If a technique is beyond the course, explain appropriately when introduced later
Does the reported accuracy follow available measurement/source precision?
Keep working precision; sensible final decimal places/significant figures.
Can I avoid repeating this routine calculation for many observations?
Show one meaningful example if needed; concise summary of other values.
Pathfinder preference: avoid lengthy tabulations; refer to traceable source or justified evidence appendix when needed. Not an IB prohibition.
What does the computed result show for the original aim and prediction? Does NEW uncertainty affect its meaning?
Interpret context and units. Refer back to earlier accuracy work unless an important new issue arises.
Don't overclaim based on an example
What mathematical question follows from this actual result, and WHY? Is an unexpected outcome worth testing first?
One evidence-led next question or warranted alternative, not simply the next planned syllabus method.
Observed result and actually available maths
Do not auto-launch an unstarted technique
MATCHING AND LAYOUT ACCEPTANCE TESTS  |  Required behaviour for the eventual student interface
Offer labelled scatter (F01) and/or concise comparison; ask whether observations actually look linear.
Do NOT automatically fit regression, calculate PMCC or show its outlier limitation at this first stage.
After graph: 'What does its shape suggest I should investigate mathematically?'
Offer common-scale side-by-side box/dot plots (F04), not repeated separated charts.
Do not force 2 long data tables, one per group.
Prompt next: compare centres/spreads with actual evidence.
Offer one relevant chart/short summary (F08); link original public source if allowed.
No long raw tables in main body OR appendices; no student-identifying source publication.
Require variable/units, source and selection explanation.
Offer labelled dimension sketch and first expression (F11), not a bar chart.
Don't require plot axes for a non-coordinate sketch; don't immediately show optimiser limitations until method used.
After sketch: explicit objective/constraint leads to function to optimise.
Offer small exact case (F16/F17), or no diagram.
No fabricated data or sampling checklist.
Define terms first, use example to motivate proof or counterexample.
Apply brief calculation checklist, not axes/title/page checks.
No penalty, do not compel a decorative figure.
Require why calculation, meaning and next step.
Student has already shown a scatter diagram
Reference original figure; new copy only if a meaningful side-by-side comparison is planned.
No duplicate figure scattered across IA.
Compare on same axis/scale and describe why repeat is necessary.
Graph cannot fit on printed page
Fail checklist; student must reflow/reformat one entire legible chart on a page.
Never split figure across two pages or shrink text beyond legibility.
Data measured to a stated precision
Ensure axis labels/reporting don't imply unsupported significant digits.
Don't manufacture extra decimals or instrument tolerances.
Link back to C24 and later results.
Prediction differs from actual plotted pattern
Record finding honestly; suggest reconsidering planned next maths.
Never force predicted normal/linear method based solely on the earlier choice.
Update investigation story, but preserve original predictions.
SOURCE / HANDOVER  ·  Use the student's confirmed Planning answers and current Data Collection notes. 'Initial exploration' is not a fixed IA writing section, nor an automatic chart generator.
